The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) Plan from the Commission on PPBE Reform Final Report. This program provides for procurement of AN/SPQ-9B radars whose primary mission is to detect and track low flying Anti-Ship Missile targets in heavy clutter. The mission of the AN/SPQ-9B has been expanded to include the capability to detect and classify periscopes. The Periscope Detection and Discrimination (PDD) capability has been designed and incorporated to operate concurrently with the Anti-Ship Missile [BR5IN AN/SPQ-9B FMP INSTALLATIONS]: AN/SPQ-9B systems are installed using Alteration Installation Teams (AITs) that customarily require funding for planning yard Design Services Allocation (DSA) up to two years prior to the year of installation and funding for Advanced Planning (AP) one year prior to installation, to support individual ship class drawing packages, ship checks and long lead material unique to the installation in order to maintain alignment with ship availability schedules. Radars continue to be procured for new construction DDGs and improvements to these and in-service systems continue to be deployed [BR6IN AN/SPQ-9B NON-FMP INSTALLATIONS]: Provided funding for the installation of equipment for Land Based Test Sites (LBTS). [P40A / BR040 TRANSMITTER UPGRADE FMP]: Funding was provided for installations of AN/SPQ-9B Transmitter Upgrades on LPD-17. [P40A / BR040 TRANSMITTER UPGRADE NON-FMP EQUIPMENT]: Funding provided for Transmitter Upgrade Processor installations at Surface Warfare Engineering Facility (SWEF) and Combat Systems Engineering Development Site (CSEDS) (both non-FMP). [P40A / BR042 AN/SPQ-9B ENGINEERING CHANGE PROPOSALS (ECP)]: Procures product improvements generated by Engineering Change Proposals (ECPs); corrects problems reported by Fleet units; upgrades unreliable components and replaces obsolete components and parts no longer in production for AN/SPQ-9B Radar; and addresses supportability concerns. Purchases and installs ECPs, including Antenna Shock Upgrade Kits, Antenna Radar Components, Digital Signal Processor (DSP) Kits, Periscope Detection and Discrimination (PDD) Kits and engineering change kit hardware components. Antenna Shock Upgrade Kits are installed during Antenna Restorations. DSP and PDD kits are installed conjunctively via Alteration Installation Team (AIT) and can be accomplished outside of a CNO Availability. [P40A / BR830 AN/SPQ-9B PRODUCTION SUPPORT]: Provides support for production of hardware and hardware components and is composed primarily of Warfare Center Activity support, Software Support Activity (SSA), Integrated Logistics Agent (ILA), Acquisition Engineering Agent (AEA), Technical Design Agent (TDA), Engineering Support Services (ESS) and Professional Support Services (PSS). Also includes support for cybersecurity compliance and software certification. [P3A / BR040 AN/SPQ-9B RADAR FMP EQUIPMENT]: Procures AN/SPQ-9B Radars to add Anti-Ship Missile Defense (ASMD) capability to Shipboard Combat Systems. Procures radars to support combat systems on the following ship classes: CG, LHA, DDG, CVN, LHD, LPD, U.S. Coast Guard National Security Cutter and a Training Unit. Systems procured for Cruisers/Destroyers (CRUDES) and Amphibious Ships in FY14 through FY21 include the Periscope Detection and Discrimination (PDD) capability. OPN Budget Line Item (BLI) 2136 consists of four separate and distinct programs, the OPNAV N96 sponsored AN/SQQ-89 Surface Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) Combat System program, the OPNAV N98 sponsored Aircraft Carrier Tactical Support Center (CV-TSC) program, the OPNAV N96 sponsored Sonar Dome Rubber Window (SDRW) program, and the OPNAV N2N6 sponsored Undersea Warfare Decision 1. AN/SQQ-89 Surface ASW Combat System (Cost Codes DB400/DB830/DB900/DB6IN): In support of the National Security Strategy (NSS), National Defense Strategy (NDS), and National Military Strategy (NMS), Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) remains a Navy core competency in a dynamic and uncertain maritime environment. U.S. adversaries continue to develop asymmetric capabilities and capacities to deter, disrupt, or delay the entry of U.S. and allied naval forces, and pose a constant challenge as the Maritime Strategy is implemented. Evolving submarine technologies offer enhanced stealth, speed, endurance, weapons, and operational proficiency, trends foretelling that the adversary submarine of the future will have a significantly larger sphere of influence, while presenting less vulnerability to ASW forces. The effective offensive engagement range of the adversary submarine of the future will continue to match or outrange individual U.S. and multinational platform sensors and weapons in many tactical environments. Submarines are an increasing threat to all Naval and Allied ships, particularly modern diesel and state-of-the-art nuclear submarines, and faster, more accurate torpedoes. Not only can the presence of potential hostile submarines delay naval combatant action until they are located and neutralized, submarines can also disrupt all seaborne logistics supply for any ground campaign as well as maritime commerce. ASW forces must be effective in all operating environments, ranging from the deep open ocean to the littorals, and are key to countering adversarial anti-access and area denial strategies. The AN/SQQ-89(V) Surface Ship ASW Combat System provides integrated Undersea Warfare (USW) combat management, fire control, command and control, and on-board training to enable surface combatants to engage USW targets in both open ocean and littoral environments. The AN/SQQ-89(V) is a system comprised of many subsystems, which integrate the helo and its sensors, the ship's own organic sensors, weapons, torpedo detection, and a high-fidelity Surface ASW Synthetic Trainer (SAST). The AN/SQQ-89A(V)15 upgrade, developed under the RDT&EN Program Element (PE) 0205620N Project 1916 Surface ASW System Improvement program, capitalizes on previously fielded AN/SQQ-89(V) systems. The AN/SQQ-89A(V)15 is comprised of a tactical towed array sensor, the Multi-Function Towed Array (MFTA), and replaces standard, militarized, legacy components with Commercial-Off-The-Shelf (COTS) hardware. The AN/SQQ-89A(V)15 features hull/towed Sonar Echo Tracker Classifier (ETC); hull/towed Sonar with Acoustic Intercept (ACI) fused data for significantly improved torpedo defense; Handling & Stowage Group (H&SG) for MFTA operation; Torpedo Setting Panel (TSP); passive towed array processing; common sub/surface sensor performance and prediction; common NAVAIR/Surface Light Airborne Multi-Purpose System (LAMPS) processing; portable software; integrated supportability; and on-board training via the Surface ASW Synthetic Trainer (SAST). Additionally, studies of the submarine and surface ASW technology show that system upgrades are most critical five to nine (5 to 9) years after each AN/SQQ-89A(V)15 installation, as failure rates within this period begin to rise. Dedicated Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) T-AGOS ships tow long acoustic arrays that collect acoustic data and relay that data to shore facilities via satellites for processing and fusion of the resulting contact data with other sensors. Currently, there are five Small Waterplane Area Twin Hull (SWATH) Passive (P)/Active (A) T-AGOS ships operating in the Pacific area. Ship configurations are: T-AGOS 22 USNS LOYAL (1), a SWATH-P platform which supports passive operations using the TB-29A Twinline (TL-29A) array, providing improved detection and classification capability. This ship class uses the Integrated Common Processor (ICP) signal processing and display system common with the SSN Acoustic Rapid Commercial Off the Shelf (COTS) Insertion (ARCI) Sonar Processing System. processing and display system, the TL-29A array, and the Compact Low Frequency Active (CLFA) transmit capability. One (1) Low Frequency Active (LFA) equipped ship, T-AGOS 23 USNS IMPECCABLE, a SWATH-A platform configured with the ICP processing and display system, the TL-29A array, and the Low Frequency Active (LFA) transmit capability. The active capability provides greatly improved detection against diesel submarines as well as the quiet nuclear submarine threat. In addition to the five platforms described above, two (2) shore sites are configured with the ICP processing and display suites to receive the T-AGOS acoustic data via Super High Frequency (SHF) satellite communication links. One of the two shore sites is equipped with three (3) SURTASS Team Trainers (STTs) to support Home Port Training Periods. A cost sharing agreement with Japan also provides two (2) shore sites and four (4) Japanese SWATH ships with similar capability to the T-AGOS SWATH-P ships for the Western Pacific region. lines.title: AN/SLQ-32
lines.text: 1810N: Other Procurement, Navy / BA 02: Communications & Electronics Equip / 2312 / AN/SLQ-32 (The following Resource Summary rows are for informational purposes only. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) AN/SLQ-32: Provides surface combatants defensive and offensive electronic warfare capabilities that are critical to ship-based layered defense. Defensive systems provide Electronic Support (ES) capability- searching for, identifying, and tracking sources of electromagnetic (EM) energy for the purpose of immediate threat recognition, targeting, planning, and conducting of future operations. ES systems complement other ship-based sensors and contribute to a surface combatant's overall picture of its threat environment. Offensive systems provide Electronic Attack (EA) capability- directing EM energy to defeat enemy fires. This non-kinetic soft-kill capability broadens ship self-defense options, deepens magazines, provides reduced logistics, and lowers "cost-per-shot" compared to kinetic munitions. AN/SLQ-32(V) is the core of surface electronic warfare (EW) capability. Navy has fielded surface electronic warfare systems designated as AN/SLQ-32(V)1-7. AN/SLQ-32(V)1-5 are legacy systems no longer in production. AN/SLQ-32(V)6 is an ES system currently in production. AN/SLQ-32(V)7, which builds on (V)6, is also in production, and it provides offensive EA at the strike group level. Scaled Onboard Electronic Attack (SOEA) is a future capability currently in development that will provide EA self-protection capability to ships unable to support AN/SLQ-32(V)7 due to size, weight, power, and cooling. The Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program (SEWIP) provides progressively greater capability through a series of block upgrades to AN/SLQ-32(V) systems: - SEWIP Block 1 provided federated Specific Emitter Identification (SEI), an upgraded console and display, and High-Gain High-Sensitivity (HGHS). (Navy recently divested of these requirements for higher priorities ). to size, weight, power, and cooling constraints. - SEWIP Block 3 provides Electronic Attack (EA) capability. Signal Processing Upgrade was previously referred to as VPX Tech Refresh. Updating the name to better describe full capability being delivered with the upgrade to the below deck equipment. Since the FY26 budget request, (V)6 VPX Upgrade Engineering Change Proposal (ECP) has been renamed AN/SLQ-32(V) Signal Processing Upgrade to more accurately describe full capability being delivered with the upgrade to the below deck equipment. The Signal Processing Upgrade is the below deck computing power behind surface EW capabilities. The Signal Processor upgrade integrates above deck hardware components with each other and the combat system. Signal Processing Upgrades are critical enablers of the added capabilities delivered by SEWIP block upgrades and next-generation countermeasures. Countermeasures are a critical component of surface EW capability and integrate with the combat system and AN/SLQ-32 via the Signal Processing Upgrade. NULKA, Long Endurance Electronic Decoy (LEED), and MK-59 soft-kill threats use EM energy to deceive a threat's guidance system. Countermeasures are funded via Budget Line Item 5530. In FY27, Navy is taking a fresh approach to acquisition of AN/SLQ-32 systems. The program office is breaking from single source contracting and instead implementing an Indefinite Delivery / Indefinite Quantity Multiple Award Contract (IDIQ MAC) strategy aimed at lowering costs and broadening the surface EW industrial base. The new contracting approach will open competition for AN/SLQ-32 production contracts by empowering industry partners to bid at the individual task order level. Industry partners will no longer be required to deliver an entire AN/SLQ-32 system. Rather, they will leverage their core competencies by delivering components of an AN/SLQ-32 system. Individual components will be integrated by Navy's organic industrial base. Block 1 + Block 2 + SOEA = Nomenclature TBD SURFACE ELECTRONIC WARFARE (EW) IMPROVEMENTS BLOCK 1: The program will divest High-Gain High-Sensitivity (HGHS Block 1B3) and Specific Emitter Identification (SEI Block 1B2) capabilities. SURFACE ELECTRONIC WARFARE (EW) IMPROVEMENTS BLOCK 2: SEWIP Block 2 provides an upgraded antenna, receiver, and combat systems interface. The upgrades will pace the evolving threat, improve detection and accuracy, and mitigate Electromagnetic Interference (EMI). The Block 2 hardware cost includes the SEWIP Block 2 ES system, Blanker-Video Mixer Group (AN/SLA-10D), Common Processing System, Common Display System, Liquid Conditioning Unit, and Data Adaptation Processor. The SEWIP Block 2, and Block 3 units are installed conjunctively to compose the AN/SLQ-32(V)7 system. AN/SLQ-32(V) Signal Processing Upgrade (previously the (V)6 VPX Upgrade Engineering Change Proposal (ECP)) provides significant capability and reliability enhancements that greatly increase the AN/ SLQ-32(V) operator's tactical situational awareness and system availability. In addition, modernization provides the back-end computing power necessary to counter emerging threats. It increases system emitter processing throughput, reduces false detections/classifications, increases system fault tolerance, simplifies system maintenance, and is a critical enabler of future artificial intelligence (AI) capability growth required to rapidly ID and classify emerging unknown threat emitters. Signal Processing Upgrade is also a pre-requisite for EW systems currently in development, such as LEED and SOEA. SURFACE ELECTRONIC WARFARE (EW) IMPROVEMENTS BLOCK 3: Block 3 provides Electronic Attack (EA) capability improvement required for the AN/SLQ-32(V) system to keep pace with the evolving threat. The equipment is procured in accordance with requirements detailed in the shipboard Information Warfare / Cryptologic System Operational Requirements Document and specific execution year fleet requirements. These requirements are defined by Fleet Cyber Command (FCC)/Commander TENTH Fleet (C10F) Fleet Signals Development Working Group (FSDWG), in concert with Shipboard Signals Exploitation Space (SSES) programs (includes Ship's Signal Exploitation Equipment Family of Systems) to ensure synergy and seamless transition to permanently installed systems. CCOP equipment is installed as an augment to cryptologic capabilities on surface units. There are approximately 120 cryptologic capable surface ships and shore sites in the current Navy inventory. Each of these are potential users of this carry-on equipment. The temporary installation of equipment is coordinated through fleet augmentation requests and installed by fleet electronic support personnel. AIS is a maritime Very High Frequency (VHF) communication system, which allows ships to exchange navigation, ship identification, and cargo information machine-to-machine via VHF transponders. AIS provides vessels with the ability to rapidly identify and track commercial shipping, which significantly increases the Navy's ability to distinguish between normal and suspicious merchant ships headed towards United States and allied ports around the globe. AIS provides critical track data to the Common Operational Picture (COP) on surface ships, AN/BYG-1 Combat System on submarines, Global Command and Control System-Maritime (GCCS-M) on Force Level ships, and Global Command and Control System-Joint (GCCS-J) at Fleet Maritime Operations Centers (MOC). The AIS submarine configuration provides an interface to the AN/BYG-1 Combat System and encrypted AIS capability. This capability dramatically improves the Combatant Commanders' situational awareness and Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) data sharing capabilities in support of regional engagement and tracking efforts against potential maritime terrorism threats. Funds will be used to continue the initial fielding of AIS (V)9 Program of Record systems, their follow-on cyber hardening upgrades, as well as the continuation of surface ship cyber hardening. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) Cooperative Engagement Capability (CEC) significantly improves Battle Force Anti-Air Warfare (AAW) capability by coordinating all Battle Force AAW sensors into a single, real-time, composite track picture capable of fire control quality. CEC distributes sensor data from each ship and aircraft, or cooperating unit (CU), to all other CUs in the battle force through a real-time, line of sight, high data rate sensor and engagement data distribution network. CEC is highly resistant to jamming and provides accurate gridlocking between CUs. Each CU independently employs high capacity, parallel processing and advanced algorithms to combine all distributed sensor data into a fire control quality track picture which is the same for all CUs. CEC data is presented as a superset of the best AAW sensor capabilities from each CU; all of which are integrated into a single input to each CU's combat weapons system. CEC significantly improves Battle Force defense in depth, including both local area and ship defense capabilities against current and future AAW threats. Moreover, CEC provides critical connectivity and integration of over-land air defense systems capable of countering emerging air threats, including land attack cruise missiles, in CEC consists of the Data Distribution System (DDS), the Cooperative Engagement Processor (CEP), and Combat System modifications. The DDS encodes and distributes ownship sensor and engagement data and is a high capacity, jam resistant, directive system providing a precision gridlocking and high throughput of data. The CEP is a high capacity distributed processor that is able to process force levels of data in near real time. This data is passed to the ship's combat system as high quality data for which the ship can cue its onboard sensors or use the data to engage targets without actually tracking them. The CEC suite contains a C-Band antenna, the antenna's power and cooling equipment, a Signal Data Processor (SDP), and system support equipment. The current CEC Shipboard antenna variants include the Shipboard Active Aperture (SBAA) and the Planar Array Antenna Assembly (PAAA). The SDP hosts the CEP software and is common across all CEC variants. The USG-2B articles in this budget procure support hardware consisting of a ruggedized 19-inch rack that contains a Cesium time standard, input/output converter, power distribution and user interface control devices. The 19-inch rack holds the SDP. SBAA and PAAA support are provided by an Antenna Environmental Control Unit (AECU) or Environmental Control System Controller (ECSC), which provide power and cooling oil to the CEC shipboard antenna. Funding provided also procures the required Weapon Replaceable Assembly (WRA) hardware required for airborne variants of CEC. CEC is planned for shipboard installations at various Naval and commercial shipyards aboard CG/CG Mod, DDG/DDG Mod, CV/CVN, LPD, LHD, DDG 1000, and LHA ship classes during scheduled ship availability periods and at land based test sites (LBTS). Advanced Tactical Data Link Systems (ATDLS) is the United States (US) Navy's only ship-to-ship/ship-to-aircraft tactical information solution equipping warfighters and Combatant Commanders with real-time battlespace data and extending the range of lethality. ATDLS is the backbone of Carrier Strike Group and AEGIS-Based Defense operations and is the key component in the fire control loop, providing critical track information for enabling maritime offense/defense, Joint Area Domain Command and Control (JADC2), Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD), Ballistic Missile Defense (BMD), Anti-Air Warfare (AAW), Anti-Surface Warfare (ASuW), Electronic Warfare (EW), Advanced Offboard Electronic Warfare (AOEW), and Long Range Fires (LRF) missions. ATDLS Integration Program develops new and improved Tactical Data Links (TDL) networking capabilities, delivering operational and targeting support to the warfighter. ATDLS rapidly and securely connects carrier/shipboard digital combat systems to military aircraft, ground troops, coalition partners, and space assets with vital Situational Awareness, targeting, and sensor information. ATDLS also provides Joint Range Extension capability via Link 16 Network (Link 16) Terminals, Command and Control Processor (C2P), and Link Monitoring and Management Tool (LMMT). C2P Technology Refresh (TR) and C2P Modernization (MOD) Full Systems Ship/Shore (DR003): C2P is the only shipboard solution that enables bi-directional exchange of tactical information across multiple TDLs within the joint operations areas. C2P processes and exchanges Link 11, Link 16, Satellite TDL J, and Joint Range Extension Applications Protocol (JREAP) tactical data among the US, North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and allied nation military platforms enabling the vital joint TDL interface. Additionally, C2P provides data translation services, acts as a single interface between host combat system and TDL networks, and forwards tactical data between platforms operating at extended ranges. C2P enables surface platforms capability to conduct Ballistic Missile Defense BMD Launch-on-Remote/Engage- on-Remote and Autonomous Vehicle missions. C2P TR with C2P v3.13 software baseline enables Tactical Targeting Network Technology (TTNT), equipping warfighters with faster network speed and improved capacity. C2P MOD procurements seamlessly cut-in starting FY26 utilizing existing contract strategy. C2P Mod delivers Link 22 capability allowing interoperability with coalition partners; as well as enabling an agile DevSecOps software deployment for rapid capability and cybersecurity upgrades, enabling continuous kill chain improvements. These upgrade kits modernize currently fielded Link 16 cabinets through two primary configurations: the Multifunctional Information Distribution System (MIDS) on-Ship (MOS) and MOS Modernization (MOS Mod). Funding starting in FY2027 includes Global Command and Control System-Maritime (GCCS-M) and the Navy fielded portions of GCCS-Joint (GCCS-J). Prior to FY2027, includes Global Command and Control System-Maritime (GCCS-M), the Navy fielded portions of GCCS-Joint. GCCS-M is the Maritime implementation of the United States (U.S.) Global Command and Control System (GCCS). It provides Maritime Commanders at all echelons of command with a single, integrated, and scalable Command, Control, Communication, Computers and Intelligence (C4I) system that fuses, correlates, filters, maintains and displays location and attributes information on friendly, hostile, and neutral land, sea, and air forces. It takes this information and integrates it with available intelligence and environmental information to support commander decision making. It operates in near real-time, constantly updating unit positions and other situational awareness data. GCCS-M also records data in appropriate databases and maintains a history of changes to those records. System operators use the data to construct relevant tactical pictures using maps, charts, topography overlays, oceanographic overlays, meteorological overlays, imagery and all-source intelligence information coordinated into a Common Operational Picture (COP) that can be shared locally and with other sites. GCCS-M v4.1.5.X provides track management for battle management aids (BMAs) critical to "Fight Tonight". Continuous delivery of GCCS-M v4.1.5 and associated training is required to support the Fleet increased demand for deployment of Carrier Strike Groups. GCCS-M is not a weapon system, but receives data from, and interfaces with Navy integrated weapons systems. Navy Commanders review and evaluate the general tactical situation, plan actions and operations, direct forces, synchronize tactical movements, and integrate force maneuver with firepower. GCCS-M operates on General Service (GENSER) Secret networks in a variety of environments and supports joint, coalition and allied forces. GCCS-M is implemented Afloat and at Ashore fixed command GCCS-Joint (GCCS-J) provides a fused picture of the battlespace within a modern command and control, communications and computer system that meets Joint warfighter and Distributed Command, Control & Communication (C3) needs. GCCS-J incorporates the core planning and assessment tools required by Combatant Commanders and their subordinate Joint Task Force Commanders to make accurate and timely decisions. GCCS-J is DoW's Joint Command and Control (C2) system of record and an essential component for successful implementation of the operational concepts of dominant maneuver, precision engagement, and full-dimension protection. GCCS-J provides situational awareness, imagery exploitation, indications and warning, collaborative planning, course-of-action development, intelligence mission support, and real-time combat execution capabilities needed to accelerate operational tempo and conduct successful military operations in the joint modern warfare environment in support of Pinnacle 27 and Fight from the Maritime Operations Center (FFTM) operations. FY27 funding also includes a one-time increase to support full hardware/software modernization of the current baseline capability at Joint Staff critical sites. This capability will provide real-time Common Operating Picture (COP) of the battlespace to support Joint and multi-national operations. Navigation Signal Timing and Ranging Global Positioning System (NAVSTAR GPS) provides assured and protected navigation solutions to Warfighters through supported, affordable, and integrated systems, and is the primary source of positioning, navigation and timing information for the Department of War (DoW). [P5 / (1R013) Navigation Warfare (NAVWAR)]: NAVWAR ensures that U.S. military forces maintain access to the GPS in an electronically challenging battlespace, delivers the capability to deny adversaries access to and use of GPS during military operations, and serves to preserve the peaceful use of GPS. Navy GPS Enhanced User Equipment (UE) Operational Requirements Document directs that future UE will incorporate an increased anti-jam capability. NAVWAR counters the threat by increasing resistance to intentional or unintentional interference. Sea NAVWAR Strategy is to install Increment 2 Advanced Digital Antenna Production (ADAP) antennas on surface platforms. The second increment also includes a smaller antenna variant for surface platforms with Size, Weight, Power and Cost (SWAP-C) restrictions. The ADAP antenna provides simultaneous dual frequency nulling and built in testability. Procurement and installation of anti-jam GPS antennas and modernized user equipment is required to ensure the continuation of GPS signals from space in a hostile jamming environment. The Sea NAVWAR program will equip ships with anti-jam GPS antennas to ensure the continued availability of GPS to support surface combat operations and provide reliable GPS and other positioning, navigation and timing data to ship-board Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (C4ISR), [P3A / (1R019) Global Positioning System (GPS)-based Positioning, Navigation, & Timing Service (GPNTS)]: The GPS-based PNT Service (GPNTS) system is the primary PNT system for the Navy to ensure reliable PNT capability and interoperability insertion in GPS receivers and associated Command, Control, Computers, Communications and Intelligence (C4I) and Combat Systems in a denied environment. GPNTS provides more robust and secure GPS/PNT capabilities than is currently in the Fleet. GPNTS provides precise PNT data required for combat, weapons, command, control, communications, navigation, and other systems, as well as providing the time synchronization critical to the network environments. GPNTS backfits current PNT/GPS systems and forward fit new platforms. GPNTS is an Open Architecture (OA) development, enabling rapid software and hardware based capability improvements to be inserted without a requirement for single-source contracting. GPNTS will host the US Space Force developed Military GPS User Equipment (MGUE) card, allowing access to the new more accurate and secure GPS Military-Code (M-Code) signal. GPNTS also provides the capability to migrate non-real time GPS data toward a Common Computing Environment (CCE) and provide a path for the integration of advanced navigation systems and sensors. Marine Air Traffic Control and Landing Systems (MATCALS) provides for continuous, all-weather, radar/non-radar approach, departure, en-route, and tower air traffic control services to an aircraft. Marine Air Traffic Control (ATC) provides initial, transition and sustained air traffic support for the Joint and Marine Air Ground Task Force air operations in any environment. MATCALS satisfies the operational requirements set forth by Specific Operational Requirements 34-22 of 12 Jul 1973; and Air Traffic Navigation Integration and Coordination System ORD 05-002 of 03 Dec 1992. MATCALS, with other Marine Air Command and Control Systems (MACCS) and federal agencies, provides the ability to project air combat power without regard to weather. ATC automation reduces air traffic controllers' traffic handling and management time, allowing more time for mission response and task accomplishment. It supports a required increase in aircraft sortie rates and contributes to extended time on target. The system provides for integration of ATC into the total MACCS. To provide this capability, MATCALS consists of 4 primary subsystems: (1) Air Traffic Navigation integration and Coordination system (ATNAVICS) AN/TPN-31(V); (2) Expeditionary Control Tower AN/TSQ-120D; (3) the Man-Portable TACAN AN/TRN-47(V)1 & 3; (4) Transportable TACAN AN/TRN-47(V)2 & 4; and various ancillary equipment. This program works with the Marine ATC Working Group identifying the requirements to implement the Pre-Planned Product Improvement (P3I) and evolutionary product improvements as required for the Ground/Air Task-Oriented Radar (G/ATOR) system, Common Aviation Command and Control System (CAC2S), ATNAVICS, Expeditionary ATC Towers, and Navigational Aids that support Marine Air Traffic Control Companies. G/ATOR is a multi-role, ground-based, expeditionary radar that replaces five legacy radar systems for the Marine Air Ground Task Force. It satisfies the Marine Air Command and Control System (MACCS) and the Ground Counter Fire / Counter Battery capabilities. Integration of ATNAVICS with the CAC2S provides a coordinated and integrated set of equipment to provide enhanced Command and Control (AC2) capability for the Tactical Air Command Center, Tactical Air Operations Center, and Direct Air Support Center to support aviation employment in Joint, combined, and coalition operations. Increased MATCALS component obsolescence of aging systems is resulting in additional Maintainability, Reliability, Improvement (MRI) costs to support the changing operational environment of the MACCS as defined by USMC Force Design 2030 dated March 2020. Evolution of MATCALS to align with the overall USN/USMC North Star Precision Approach Landing Capability (PALC) to provide landing capability in both contested and non-contested environments via non-radar and radar based systems. The Joint DoW/Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) National Airspace System (NAS) Modernization (MOD) program upgrades the DoW ATC systems at approach control facilities in concert with the FAA's upgrade of the National ATC System. These funds will procure ATC systems for the Navy/Marine ATC facilities. The Air Force is the DoW lead activity for the Joint Acquisition Program. The Joint Program Office NAVAIR provides shore based ATC terminal facilities with equipment that is required in joint efforts to efficiently and safely monitor and direct military and commercial air traffic in national and international air space. Many of these systems are required to interface through automated means with the FAA. Additionally, NAVAIR has material support responsibility for Special Instrumentation Systems, and Ancillary Equipment used at Navy and Marine Corps Aviation Shore activities in the continental United States and overseas. Future upgrades and replacement systems will be performed under the NASMOD NAS Voice System budget line. Emergency Communication System (ECS) Upgrade Program (MR445) - This program modernizes obsolete and unsupportable ECS equipment. Voice Switches, Recorders, Reproducers, Uninterruptable Power Supplies, and Built-In Test Equipment will be replaced with modern, supportable components and procurements were completed in FY 2020 and installations completed in FY 2022. Future upgrades and replacement systems will be performed under the NASMOD NAS Voice System budget line. Air Field Lighting Control System (AFLCS) (MR510) - This program modernizes obsolete and unsupportable AFLCS equipment which will be replaced with modern, supportable components. Funding for this effort was realigned to the Terminal Automation System (TAS) CB070 beginning in FY 2018. The TAS provides the functionality and meets the requirements of the airfield lighting control as prescribed in the NASMOD ORD III Airfield Automation Annex A dated 16MAR05. The AFLCS circuitry will be incorporated into the Visual Information Display System (VIDS) as part of the VIDS Tech Refresh Program under the Operational Communication System (OCS)/Emergency Communication System (ECS) Air Traffic Control (ATC) Recorder replacement program (MR520) - Through participation in the FAA ATC recorder replacement program will replace aging and obsolete ATC OCS and ECS ATC recorders with state of the art ATC recording/reproducing technology. Fiber Optic Communications Intersite System (FOCIS) Upgrade Program (MR530) - FOCIS is required for Precision Approach Radar (PAR) operations and for ATC voice communications at Naval and Marine Corps ATC facilities. This program modernizes obsolete and unsupportable FOCIS equipment with modern supportable components. Landing Systems budget provides funding to modernize and ensure the reliability of Precision Approach Radars (PAR), Tactical Air Navigation (TACAN) systems, Instrument Landing Systems (ILS), and other air navigation aids used by the Navy and Marine Corps. lines.text: 1810N: Other Procurement, Navy / BA 02: Communications & Electronics Equip / 2830 / Afloat ATC Equipment (The following Resource Summary rows are for informational purposes only. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) SATC systems are responsible for safe and expeditious control of air traffic within 50 Nautical Miles of a ship. SATC systems include the air traffic surveillance radar (ASR), AN/SPN43 and the air traffic control processing and display system, AN/TPX-42A(V), which has two major configurations: AN/TPX-42A(V)15/16. The (V)16 configurations comprise of Carrier Air Traffic Control Center - Direct Altitude and Identity Readout (CATCC-DAIR), Amphibious Air Traffic Control Center - Direct Altitude and Identity Readout (AATCC-DAIR); (V)16 DAIR system is used with the AN/SPN-43 and Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) inputs to track and control aircraft. The second configuration, AN/TPX-42A(V)15 interfaces with next generation multipurpose radars and IFF to perform the same mission. Obsolescence problems are being addressed through various upgrades in a phased approach. The major upgrades include a series of AN/TPX-42A(V) modification kits requiring various combinations of OL-541processor re-host, track processor upgrade, OD-220 console, audio/video recorder, flat panel display, embedded trainer, and other components to bring the AN/TPX-42A(V)16 through execution of the Air Traffic Control Multifunction Console Engineering Change Proposal (ECP), to the AN/SYY-1 configuration. The nomenclature AN/SYY-1 more accurately reflects the system attributes as a (S) water (Surface Ship), (Y) data processing, (Y) surveillance and control system. The ASR capability provided by the AN/SPN-43 radar system is required for NIMITZ Class CVNs and LHA/LHD class ships until the capability is replaced by the AN/SPN-50 Shipboard Air Traffic Radar. Obsolescence problems are being addressed through various upgrades in a phased approach until replaced. Shipboard Air Traffic Radar (SATR) (AN/SPN-50(V)) The "National Defense Strategy of the United States of America" calls for military forces to assure allies and friends, dissuade potential adversaries, deter aggression and counter coercion, and defeat adversaries in order to accomplish our national objectives. The Shipboard Air Traffic Radar (SATR) AN/SPN-50(V) supports these objectives and will be the primary Air Traffic Control (ATC) surveillance radar onboard Nimitz Class Aircraft Carrier (CVN) and Amphibious (LHA and LHD) type ships. The launch and recovery of aircraft, to include ATC, is a primary function of aircraft carriers and amphibious landing platforms. The surveillance function provides weather and radar data to air traffic controllers supporting aviation operations of all Navy, Marine Corps, joint and allied aviation assets within the assigned airspace. This data is utilized by air traffic controllers to provide a variety of ATC services such as ATC radar approach and departure services, which includes aircraft separation, airspace monitoring, navigational assistance, emergency vectoring, traffic calls, and vectoring and sequencing to the final approach point. Reliable and accurate ATC surveillance radar enhances overall mission and training effectiveness, and safety for aircrews and aircraft alike. The AN/SPN-50(V) CDD was signed March 2015 and Milestone B was achieved September 2015 where the Milestone Decision Authority (MDA) designated the AN/SPN-50(V) Program as an ACAT IV(T). The AN/SPN-50(V) CPD was signed November 2018. Milestone C was achieved September 2020, and IOC was achieved 3rd quarter FY 2024. The AN/SPN-50(V) inventory objective is 25 systems (20 LRIP and 5 FRP). ACLS Mod Kits comprises three legacy systems (AN/SPN-46, AN/SPN-41, and AN/SPN-35C) that provide the primary and secondary precision electronic guidance for landing suitably equipped aircraft under all weather conditions on CVNs, LHA/LHD class ships, and selected Naval Air Stations. Many of the components in the system have been in service for more than thirty years. This program funds maintainability, reliability, modernization and supportability improvements to existing equipment components that can no longer be maintained, procured or supported, as well as items providing upgraded capability and improved operational relevance in more environments. Life Cycle Extension (LCE) sustainment efforts for ACLS systems will be completed to address obsolescence and supportability issues, leverage Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) technology, address cyber-security updates and requirements, and support external system interface requirements. The LCE efforts by system are planned to be conducted in blocks, to address the most critical obsolescence, supportability, and emergent requirements first and to group remaining improvements into logical block upgrade packages that minimize multiple, duplicative repair efforts and reduce costs while delivering hardware in a time phased approach to meet ship maintenance availability schedules. This program includes a shore-based variant, installed at key airfields, that provides identical control signal indications (for pilot familiarization) as those provided by the afloat systems on board CVN vessels. In 2022, the Navy approved an updated Precision Approach and Landing Capability (PALC) Roadmap that planned to field system upgrades aimed at modernizing the AN/SPN-35 and AN/SPN-46 systems as well as inserting common sub-systems that minimize future sustainment costs. In 1QFY2025, the 2022 PALC Roadmap update was rescinded and the AN/SPN-51 development was halted. With no planned replacement system, it is essential to continue fielding Radar Landing System (RLS) mod kits that address subsystem obsolescence issues and extend the systems' life until a replacement system is identified. These mod kits support all three radar-based landing systems: AN/SPN-46 Automated Carrier Landing System (ACLS), AN/SPN-41 Instrument Carrier Landing System (ICLS), and AN/SPN-35 Precision Approach Radar (PAR). The life cycle extension and obsolescence modification kit approach aligns with the guidance provided in the original 2013 PALC Roadmap that identified system service life requirements AN/SPN-46 Automatic Carrier Landing System (ACLS) is a Precision Approach Landing System (PALS) on board CVN class ships that provides aircraft position information to the Final Control Workstation in Carrier Air Traffic Control Center (CATCC) and provides the pilot with the capability of selecting a fully automatic, instrument landing, or talk down approach. Aircraft communications are available to aircraft equipped with the AN/APN-245 Beacon (or a successor system). The AN/SPN-46 system is certified to provide the carrier with an all-weather flight operational capability. Initial Operational Capability (IOC) of the AN/SPN-46 was in 1985, and the system has exceeded its design life. There are significant obsolescence issues. AN/SPN-46 Block IV upgrade is designed to correct known obsolescence issues in the antenna pedestal, modulator/transmitter, and various Circuit Card Assemblies (CCAs). If this effort is not accomplished, replacement parts will not be available to support the system, thereby, negatively affecting Operational Availability (Ao) and safety of flight on the aircraft carrier. Similarly, AN/SPN-46 Block V upgrades address obsolete equipment hardware and software, specifically processor CCAs, Real Time Operating System (RTOS), and radar software. These installations are required to sustain the systems aboard ships until 2040. Without these collective upgrades, system Operational Availability (Ao) and aircraft safety of flight will be significantly, negatively affected. AN/SPN-41 Instrument Carrier Landing System (ICLS) transmitting set provides all weather instrument approach guidance from the ship to the aircraft equipped with AN/ARA-63 Receiver Group (or a successor system). It is a secondary precision electronic landing system and safety of flight back up to provide azimuth and elevation alignment information to suitably equipped aircraft aboard CVN and LHA/LHD class ships. Initial Operational Capability (IOC) of the AN/SPN-41 was in 1970 and the system has exceeded its design life. AN/SPN-41 LCE upgrades previously include the Transmitter, Coder Monitor, Electronics Drawer, and Radome hardware to ensure continued operational availability and extended service life of the AN/SPN-41. Current and future upgrades include a AN/SPN-41 Solid State Transmitter, that replaces legacy magnetron transmitters responsible for degraded system reliability, as well as various modification kit upgrades, that address obsolescence in the equipment operating systems and their associated The AN/SPN-41 systems on LHA/LHD class ships have been placed in an "Inactive Equipment Maintenance (IEM)" status and will be removed, as needed, to maintain the AN/SPN-41 capability on CVN class AN/SPN-35C is the Precision Approach Radar aboard LHA/LHD class ships and is used for Mode III aircraft recovery, which ensures the safe approach and landing of fixed and rotary wing aircraft during adverse weather and night conditions. Original AN/SPN-35 equipment was built and installed in the 1960s and Initial Operational Capability (IOC) of the AN/SPN-35C was in 2004. The AN/SPN-35C Block II addressed modernization of the legacy AN/SPN-35C with the development of Active Electronic Scanned Array (AESA) equipment, that also addressed obsolescence and operational limitations of the existing receiver-transmitter, pedestal, antenna group, and stabilization subsystem. The 2022 PALC Roadmap update directed realignment of this upgrade to the AN/SPN-51 Brizo Landing System. With the subsequent cancellation of AN/SPN-51 Brizo Landing System development efforts, sub-system Life-Cycle Extension upgrades are being pursued to extend overall system service life to 2040. Without the development and fielding of sub-system upgrades, system Ao and aircraft safety of flight will be significantly, negatively affected. lines.text: 1810N: Other Procurement, Navy / BA 02: Communications & Electronics Equip / 2867 / Joint Precision Approach and Landing System(JPALS) (The following Resource Summary rows are for informational purposes only. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) The Joint Precision Approach and Landing System (JPALS) is the primary precision approach and landing system for CVN and LHA/D ships to support aircraft without SPN-46 Automatic Carrier Landing Systems (ACLS) capability, which include F-35B, F-35C, MQ-25, CVM-22 and future platforms. The nomenclature for JPALS has been designated AN/USN-3(V)1, Satellite Signals Landing System (SSLS). JPALS ship systems are required to provide CVN and LHA/D ships a primary precision approach capability during night and instrument flight conditions, including coupled approach capability to a hover transition point for LHA/D ships, and coupled approach to the deck (auto-land) capability aboard CVN ships, and in contested environments. JPALS also provides over-the-air inertial alignment capability for CVN and LHA/D ships to support aircraft platforms without Link-4A capability, including F-35, MQ-25, CVM-22 and future platforms. JPALS MS B occurred June 2016 and MS C occurred April 2019. lines.text: 1810N: Other Procurement, Navy / BA 02: Communications & Electronics Equip / 2876 / Naval Mission Planning Systems (The following Resource Summary rows are for informational purposes only. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) This line item provides funding to procure Mission Planning workstations and associated Support Equipment, Software/Production Engineering Support, and Integrated Logistics Support (ILS) for the Naval Mission Planning Systems (NavMPS) family of systems. The NavMPS family of systems includes the Joint Mission Planning System-Maritime (JMPS-M), Collaborative Mission Planning Continuum (CMPC) formerly called Next Generation Naval Mission Planning System (NGNMPS), JMPS-E (Expeditionary), Electronic Kneeboard (EKB), Common Munitions Built-in-Test (BIT)/Reprogramming Equipment (CMBRE), Standardized Tester of Reprogrammable Munitions (STORM, formerly called "Next Generation CMBRE"), and Common Munitions Built-in-Test (BIT)/Reprogramming Equipment Cyber Enhanced (CMBRE CE) JMPS-M (Maritime) is the legacy automated mission planning system for Naval Aviation, currently supporting over 40 Type/Model/Series (T/M/S) U.S. Navy and Marine Corps aircraft and expeditionary forces. The JMPS-M program support includes platforms such as: F/A-18 A/B/C/D/E/F, EA-18G, CH-53K, Marine Helicopters, H-60 R/S, and P-8A. JMPS-M enables weapon system employment by providing the information and decision aids needed to rapidly plan aircraft, weapon or sensor missions, load mission data into aircraft and weapons, conduct mission rehearsal, and post mission analysis. The Naval Aviation's modern aircraft need data loaded from JMPS-M to fly their missions. The JMPS-M system procures hardware and software assets at all appropriate classification levels to support mission-planning requirements. The JMPS-M system is sun-setting in FY 2027 with a transition to CMPC. The Collaborative Mission Planning Continuum (CMPC) formerly called Next Generation Naval Mission Planning System (NGNMPS), will address critical capability gaps and deficiencies in the legacy JMPS that are required for modern 21st century integrated mission-centric and collaborative multi-domain mission planning, execution and analysis. The CMPC will begin replacing Naval Aviation's legacy JMPS no later than FY 2027 while also affordably leveraging prior investments across the systems of systems to deliver integrated and collaborative capability. The CMPC will address technological obsolescence while delivering enhanced capabilities to support the current Air Wing and the Air Wing of the future. The CMPC capability provides advanced multiple aircraft planning capabilities focused on emerging, high-threat mission areas. Current mission planning capabilities support individual aircraft and weapon initialization requirements. The emerging, near-peer threat environment demands a much more capable system that enables a team of aircraft to cooperate effectively across multiple mission areas, domains, and security levels. The CMPC will also leverage modernized architecture to provide revolutionary improvements in workflow, usability, cybersecurity. Additionally, CMPC will provide information and decision aids needed to rapidly plan/employ/maximize effectiveness of aircraft/weapon/sensor/payload mission plans. This functionality includes advanced pre-mission rehearsal/analysis, loading mission data into aircraft and weapons, dynamic replanning/retargeting against evolving threats in contested environments, and advanced post-mission debrief/ analysis. The CMPC will incorporate cross-domain solution capabilities. The CMPC system will also conduct work support advanced technology maturation, risk reduction activities, and system demonstrations supporting future mission planning needs for both USN and USMC users. These mission planning, mission execution, and mission analysis functions will be designed to meet the National Defense Strategy objectives. The CMPC will conduct preflight mission planning, data loading, rehearsals, mission execution and post mission analyses at all appropriate security classification levels. JMPS-E (Expeditionary) is a scalable, tailorable and collaborative web-based mission planning and execution monitoring tool for Marine Expeditionary Unit and Amphibious Squadron staffs embarked with each Amphibious Ready Group (ARG) and Expeditionary Strike Group (ESG). The EKB provides Naval Aviation with a scalable, rapidly deployable capability to support Department of War (DoW) digital transformation initiatives. The EKB is configured on a commercially available portable electronic device and contains digital flight information, aeronautical products, reference material, and flight planning tools to support aviation operations in land-based, littoral, and blue-water environments. The EKB also provides tactical mission planning and execution capabilities including tactical decision aids that support the range of Naval Aviation Enterprise (NAE) operations. The EKB has two baseline configurations - an unclassified Electronic Flight Bag (EFB) device and the Tactical Flight Bag (TFB) device, which is currently classified up to Secret after loading mission-specific software. The EFB's function is to support flight planning and execution while the TFB's function is to support tactical mission employment. The EKB effort addresses a high-priority fleet "paperless cockpit" initiative which reduces the number of printed paper-based products needed for in-flight use while also accommodating the need to store and display data to the operator necessary to execute training and tactical missions. EKB funding provides at least one operational EKB device per aircraft cockpit seat based on Primary Aircraft Authorization (PAA) requirements. The CMBRE system provides USN/USMC forces with the critical capability to perform built-in-test (BIT) and programming/reprogramming of various weapons both afloat and ashore. The CMBRE system operations afloat require the modernization of ammunition Magazine Operations (MAGOPS) in all aircraft carriers (CVN-68 and CVN-78 classes) as well as large-deck L-Class (LHA/LHD) amphibious assault ships; The MAGOPS capability enables safe BIT checks and programming/reprogramming of stores in shipboard magazines to support enhanced sortie generation requirements. The STORM/CMBRE CE is the follow-on replacement system for the legacy CMBRE System. The STORM/CMBRE CE system addresses legacy CMBRE end of life obsolescence issues while also modernizing the system into an affordable, lightweight, compact, modular design. The STORM/CMBRE CE system further supports USMC expeditionary mission requirements, mandatory cybersecurity protections and resilience, and data transfer speeds that are required to support air wing combat readiness. Further STORM/CMBRE CE supports advanced Net-Enabled Weapons across the enterprise that are required in support of the National Defense Strategy (NDS) to pace the emerging threat. The STORM/CMBRE CE system will affordably enhance mission readiness and security, generate improved flexibility, depth and capacity for existing and emerging aviation weapon capabilities during the conduct of ship, shore, and ship-to-shore operations in both conventional and Disaggregated Aviation Operating (DAO) environments. The STORM/CMBRE CE program is not experiencing cost growth, the increase is due to the transition from a Section 804 Middle Tier of Acquisition rapid prototyping to an ongoing program of record. The STORM/CMBRE CE Production Hardware Units replace the legacy CMBRE system and provides the USN/USMC the ability to perform built-in-test and programming/reprogramming of various weapons. Funding FY 2027 will continue the procurement of STORM/CMBRE CE products to meet mandatory cyber security requirements, affordably address obsolescence, and meet emergent operational requirements including support for Disaggregated Aviation Operations supporting the National Defense Strategy. STORM/CMBRE CE hardware will maintain mission readiness, fleet readiness, and affordable system sustainability. Increase in FY 2027 is due to continuation of program of record and associated procurement of production assets. STORM/CMBRE CE Production Engineering Support provides engineering production drawings, parts and assembly, as well as engineering change proposals / updates to the STORM/CMBRE CE system. Efforts include implementation of cybersecurity mandates as well as addressing emergent cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Increase in Engineering Support corresponds to additional required support for STORM/CMBRE CE Integrated Logistics Support provides technical documentation, training materials, and installation / operation instructions for the STORM/CMBRE CE system. The STORM/CMBRE CE Program documentation is compliant with cybersecurity mandates and Communications Tasking Orders for newly deployed platforms. Increase in Logistics Support corresponds to additional required support for STORM/CMBRE CE Production Acceptance Testing supports production acceptance testing of manufactured units prior to Fleet delivery. As aircraft and weapons become increasingly advanced, they will require increased access, quantity, processing analysis and fidelity of data to support mission planning, mission execution, dynamic mission re- planning and mission analysis. These data requirements will require additional advanced processors, memory, storage, and servers. Mission Planning Seats refer to the computer workstations that employ the mission planning software. Program cost is not directly related to FY hardware quantity; software is a cost factor independent of FY hardware quantity and cost. Funding profile accounts for required four-year workstation refresh cycle to preclude aging/obsolete hardware and reduce failure rates, procure supporting emerging technology such as EKB (and STORM/CMBRE CE starting in FY 2024) to support advanced operational capabilities and address system obsolescence/cybersecurity requirements/mission readiness requirements, and support memory requirements for high-end mission planning capabilities. lines.text: 1810N: Other Procurement, Navy / BA 02: Communications & Electronics Equip / 2900 / Maritime Integrated Broadcast System BSA 10: Other Shore Electronic Equipment (The following Resource Summary rows are for informational purposes only. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) Funding for Maritime Integrated Broadcast System (MIBS) has been realigned out of line item 2900 into line item 2361 starting in FY 2026. This is to consolidate the number of program elements (PE) and budget line items (BLI) to group technology projects to allow flexibility fostering innovation and efficiency. PE/BLI consolidation meets the DoD Implementation Plan from the Commission on PPBE Final Report. The MIBS program delivers Integrated Broadcast Service (IBS) data to operational and tactical decision makers aboard United States Navy surface ships, shore headquarters, and other joint platforms. MIBS provides the Navy with the capability to receive and deliver near real time, Over the Air (OTA) IBS data, enhancing the Common Operation Picture (COP) supporting operations in all warfare areas. Including Ballistic Missile Defense (BMD), Anti-Air Warfare (AAW), Anti-Surface Warfare (ASUW), Undersea Warfare (UW), Electronic Warfare (EW) and track location of red and blue forces to warfighters at the tactical edge, regardless of Emission Control (EMCON) posture. MIBS provides essential support to the Over the Horizon-Targeting (OTH-T) mission and supports closure of the kill chain in a denied environment. This budget will provide a technical refresh of the Joint Tactical Terminal - Maritime (JTT-M) systems. The Joint Tactical Terminal - Maritime Evolved (JTT-ME) system replaces an End of Life (EoL) JTT- Senior terminals and infrastructure with a modern, secure, network enabled infrastructure that allows flexibility for future radios/waveforms. This system is formally specified by Fleet Commanders as a threshold capability for global Maritime Command, Control and Communications in a Distributed Maritime Environment to execute current Warfighting plans and is required for National Command and Control capability. The MIBS program will replace the End of Life (EoL) JTT-Senior radio (JTT-M) that has been in sustainment for 20+ years. Tactical/Mobile (TacMobile) Command, Control, Communications, Computers, and Intelligence (C4I) Systems: TacMobile is the ground station program that supports P-8A Poseidon and MQ-4C Triton pre and post-flight C4I requirements and Inflight Command and Control support. These ground stations provide critical reach-back capabilities between the airborne platforms and the Maritime Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) Enterprise/ decision makers. TacMobile consists of fixed-site Tactical Operations Centers (TOCs), Mobile Tactical Operations Centers (MTOCs), and Fly Away Kits (FAKs). TOCs are located at major Maritime Patrol and Reconnaissance Aircraft (MPRA) Continental United States (CONUS) and deployment hub sites. MTOCs are scalable, mobile versions of the TOC used for extended contingency operations at remote forward operating bases, while FAKs are small transportable systems that support emergent short term detachments for limited duration. a) 6 TOCs: Systems located at Naval Air Station (NAS) Jacksonville, Florida; NAS Sigonella, Italy; Marine Corps Base Hawaii (MCBH) Kaneohe Bay, Hawaii; NAS Whidbey Island, Washington; Naval Air Facility (NAF) Kadena, Japan; and Isa Air Base Bahrain. d) 1 Schoolhouse located at the Center for Naval Air Technical Training Unit (CNATT-U) NAS Jacksonville, Florida. The TacMobile program is comprised of 23 subsystems that utilize an evolutionary development strategy consisting of incremental upgrades synchronized to match increased P-8A capabilities while retaining current functionality and readiness. Incremental upgrades and tech refreshes are planned to support the Maritime Patrol and Reconnaissance Force (MPRF) Family of Systems aircraft advances. TacMobile Acquisition strategy is to modernize the Computers, Communications, Command, Control, and Intelligence (C4I) architecture that implements a modular system design approach allowing for rapid upgrades to system capabilities to keep pace with evolving operational environments. The modular design approach also allows for the fielding of incremental capability packages (CP-1, CP-2, CP-3). TacMobile 2.1.2 Tech Refresh upgrades the Communications equipment in order to address End-of-Life (EOL) issues, Interim P-8A Ground Station (PGS), and TacMobile Capability Packages over the Future Years Defense Program (FYDP). The communications equipment includes Ultra High Frequency (UHF)/Very High Frequency (VHF) satellite radios and Super High Frequency (SHF) voice and data communications systems. Tech refresh also includes Tactical Mobile Advanced Airborne Sensor (TMAAS) Interface Kit (TIK) to support Advanced Airborne Sensor (AAS) operations worldwide and Tactical Mobile Acoustic Support System (TacMASS) upgrade to support Post Flight Analysis of Acoustic Intelligence Data. TacMobile Tech Refresh 2.1.3 is Capability Package 1 (CP-1), which modernizes the Secret domain C4I architecture, leverages 2.1.2 Tech Refresh equipment, leveraging applicable P-8A Ground Station (PGS) components, and provides risk reduction for TacMobile Increment 3 at non-PGS units. CP-1 modernizes the C4I server stack using converged network attached storage which increases data storage and improves maintainability while also reducing Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP). Implementing a services-based architecture that leverages Platform as a Service (PaaS) and Software as a Service (SaaS) technology using containerized applications, this modernization facilitates speed to capability, increased agility and reliability, and better quality and maintainability of TacMobile software with improved Cyber resilience. Additionally, Tech Refresh 2.1.3 modernizes legacy Fly Away Kits (FAK) to maintain alignment with P-8A aircraft Fleet Release modernization. Funding for PGS is aligned under Program Element (PE) 0204251N and will be executed by Budget Submitting Office (BSO) N00019 PEO Air ASW, Assault and Special Mission Programs to support the initial deployments until the final follow on TacMobile Inc 3 system is fielded. The full TacMobile Inc 3 systems will leverage the PGS architecture with a focus on increased mobility (Size, Weight, Power and Cost (SWaP-C)) and cloud-based architecture at multi-security classification levels that meet TacMobile Inc 3's full Capability Production Document (CPD) requirements. System architecture improvements, Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) and Anti Surface Warfare (ASuW) sensor improvements, SATCOM capability upgrades, an ASuW Net Enabled Weapon, and a Higher- Than-Secret security capability. PGS provides the timely support to P-8A ECP 6/7 configured aircraft to conduct preflight mission planning, operate within SECRET and Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) enclaves, perform in-flight Command and Control (C2) mission support, and conduct post flight debriefing and sensor data dissemination. This effort also funds fleet prioritized requirements as a part of the Rapid Capability Insertion (RCI) process to pace the global ASW and ASuW threats and address reliability improvements, obsolescence, periodic technology insertion, correction of deficiencies, including funds to implement various changes at Tactical Operations Centers (TOCs) and Mobile Tactical Operations Centers (MTOCs) to improve systems reliability and cyber security. Deployable Joint Command and Control (DJC2) (JH500): DJC2 is a rapidly deployable, self-contained, and network-enabled system that provides mission command capabilities in expeditionary environments, such as disaster relief or forward-deployed operations. It enables commanders to set up a fully functional, secure, and powered operations center anywhere in the world within 6-24 hours in direct support of Global Response Force (GRF) and emerging Fleet requirements leveraging DJC2's Fly Away Kits (FAKs) to meet mission requirements and fill capability gaps. Utilizing a fielded DJC2 system, the commander and staff can securely communicate across the world, send and receive information across five different computer networks (including secure networks and the Internet), participate in video teleconferences with remote locations, and use a fully integrated command and control/collaboration software tool suite to plan and execute missions. The JROC-approved 2008 Capabilities Program Directive mandates a 5-year refresh cycle for this Information Technology system, (18-24 months per the CPD), with the DJC2 program serving as steward to ensure system capabilities remain aligned with Priority Critical Cybersecurity requirements and Deployable Distributed Command, Control & Communications (C3) capabilities. lines.text: 1810N: Other Procurement, Navy / BA 02: Communications & Electronics Equip / 2914 / Intelligence Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) BSA 10: Other Shore Electronic Equipment (The following Resource Summary rows are for informational purposes only. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) The Distributed Common Ground Systems- Navy (DCGS-N) is a cooperative effort between the services, agencies, and the Department of War (DoW) to provide systems capable of receiving, processing, exploiting, and disseminating data from airborne and national reconnaissance platforms. DCGS-N is the Navy instance of the Under Secretary of War, Intelligence (USW (I)) DCGS Family of Systems (FoS). The DoW has defined a DCGS architecture that will be compatible and interoperable across all of the Services Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) systems and operations. DCGS accesses and ingests data from space borne, airborne, subsurface, and surface ISR collection assets, intelligence databases, and intelligence producers. Integration with the Common Data Fabric (CDF) will enhance access and sharing of ISR information across Joint forces using common enterprise standards and services. DCGS FoS supports Joint Task Force (JTF)-level and below combat operations with critical intelligence for battle management and information dominance to maintain a tactical advantage over adversaries. DCGS-N Afloat and Ashore systems fulfill a critical mission set Afloat and Ashore. DCGS-N processes and exploits tactical and Imagery Intelligence (IMINT), Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT), and Signals Intelligence (SIGINT); facilitates precision target geopositioning, mensuration, and imagery capabilities; integrates national IMINT requirements and processing capabilities from the National Geospatial- Intelligence Agency (NGA), and shares Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance, and Targeting (ISR&T) and Command and Control information via the DIB, Defense Intelligence Information Enterprise (DI2E), and Net-Centric Enterprise Services (NCES) standards with a wide range of customers. The DCGS-N program conducts research and assessments of tactically relevant, emerging technologies for program insertion to ensure superiority in the intelligence domain. The DCGS-N Enterprise Node (DEN) facilitates interoperability and data sharing among the DCGS FoS. DCGS-N provides software integration prior to installation and complies with the DoW DCGS network architecture. [P5 - 2 / Intelligence Carry-On Program (ICOP)]: 5E004: Intelligence Carry-On Program (ICOP) is a suite of multi-source intelligence and analytical capabilities that includes an integrated Three-Dimensional (3-D) operational picture displaying intelligence and other data sources to provide a richer and more complete picture of the battle space on Unit Level platforms. The system supports a Full Motion Video (FMV) capability that receives, processes, exploits, and disseminates organic and non-organic data as well as the ability to process and correlate Electronic Intelligence (ELINT) and external Communications Intelligence (COMINT Externals). It integrates a menu of mature Commercial Off-the-Shelf (COTS) and Government Off-the-Shelf (GOTS) applications with shared storage and communication paths to reach back to the DEN, and to provide data sharing to the Maritime Operations Centers (MOC) and National ISR systems, making tactical users a part of the larger ISR enterprise. ICOP provides Indications and Warnings (I&W), battlespace awareness/visualization, pattern of life analysis, FMV and ISR Processing, Exploitation and Dissemination (PED) capabilities in support of Unit-Level Navy surface (CG, DDG, LPD, FFG, and DDG 1000 classes) and expeditionary operations. The ICOP system includes a three-eyed ruggedized workstation that serves as a powerful afloat edge computing device that is capable of operating on all three security domains (NIPR, SIPR and JWICs) and an antenna/receiver set (called Communications Module 3 - CM3) that is used to ingest, process and exploit airborne sensor data. In addition to supporting multi-intelligence capabilities, Intelligence Carry-On Program (ICOP)/Communications Module 3 (CM3) provides an end-to-end Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) PED architecture that includes processing organic shipboard camera systems to support Navy-wide Operational Task (OPTASK) Visual Information (Strategic Communications - "First to the Truth," pattern of life analysis and use of force/rules of engagement decisions). For procurement activities, Intelligence Carry-On Program (ICOP) satisfies Unit-Level requirements as part of the Distributed Common Ground System - Navy (DCGS-N) Family of Systems (FoS). ICOP has been designated as a Navy equipage system (carry on/carry off). ICOP employs a cross-decking methodology by drawing from a rotatable pool of workstations to support the total inventory objective. The ICOP workstation and CM3 antenna/receivers are considered carry on/carry off equipment while the supporting infrastructure to mount the systems is considered permanent infrastructure. Government Off-the-Shelf (GOTS) technologies in order to streamline Sailor's analytical efforts and improve targeting solutions for the operator, optimizing and compressing the kill chain. DCGS-N Increment 2 will deliver all source fusion and analytical capabilities; provide Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) capabilities and integrate Tasking, Collection, Processing, Exploitation, and Dissemination (TCPED) capabilities to optimize the use and analysis of sensor and platform data. DCGS-N Increment 2 leverages enterprise solutions to share information across commands, services, and agencies to promote shared situational awareness. DCGS-N Increment 2 consists of multiple releases that build upon capability over time and allow for ongoing fleet feedback as the software matures. DCGS-N Increment 2 will insert new technology enhancements via incremental software upgrades. Continued development of follow-on releases will be based on prioritized Fleet requirements. DCGS-N Increment 2 addresses a critical shortfall in TCPED capability and capacity to support operational, tactical planning, and execution across the full range of joint military operations. Existing TCPED shortfalls will be exacerbated by planned Navy, Joint, and Allied fielding of new Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) platforms. Currently fielded systems provide localized processing capabilities that will be overwhelmed in future years without a significant change in the way the Navy processes, exploits and disseminates intelligence data. Consolidated Afloat Networks and Enterprise Services (CANES) operates at the Tactical Edge which is defined as "The platforms, sites, and personnel (U. The corresponding budget requests are documented elsewhere.) General Purpose Electrical/Electronic Test Equipment (GPETE) funding is provided to execute a detailed, multi-year sustainment and modernization plan for intermediate and organizational maintenance activities. GPETE is the equipment employed to ensure the accuracy of installation, alignment, and maintenance (preventative and routine) of all Navy weapons systems ashore and afloat. The GPETE procured must meet rigid technical requirements, be cost effective, and satisfy valid deficiencies in authorized allowance. Within the Test, Measurement, and Diagnostic Equipment (TMDE) program, GPETE is classified under 4 functional groups: Fiber Optics (M6000), Signal Generators (M6001), Oscilloscopes & Meters (M6002), and Passive/Ancillary/Mechanical (M6004). The program also breaks out a fifth cost code (M6003) for non-equipment (i.e. labor) tasks including engineering, procurement and integrated logistics support. The Test, Measurement, and Diagnostic Equipment (TMDE) program procures Commercial-off-the- Shelf (COTS; i.e. non-government manufactured test equipment that is available to the general public) GPETE to address the maintenance requirements across shipboard/shore- based activities and programs. Approximately 90% of the annual test equipment requirements are procured through the DoW Supply System, or MILSTRIP, process. When the program procures through Military Standard Requisitioning and Issue Procedures (MILSTRIP), the Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) or Naval Supply Systems Command Weapon Systems Support (NAVSUP WSS) fills the requisition. The remaining 10% of procurements are Simplified Acquisition Purchase (SAP) contracts or purchase card buys. SAP and purchase card requisitions are utilized only for obsolete test equipment that is no longer available for procurement through MILSTRIP. Any variance in unit costs and quantity across fiscal years is attributable to the diversity and varying complexity of the COTS GPETE to be procured from year to year to address the maintenance requirements across shipboard/shore- based activities and programs. A portion of the cost growth from FY to FY within the cost codes can be attributed to an average industry cost growth. Any average unit cost code growth beyond 2% would be the result of planned procurements of larger quantities of more complex/capable GPETE and/or modernization to more complex/capable GPETE, which tend to be more expensive. The Navy's inventory of GPETE is approaching obsolescence and requires modernization to avoid deterioration in the accuracy of our weapons systems. Many models are no longer in production, so replacement equipment must be purchased from newer model inventory, some of which have a greater unit cost. Failure to maintain accurate test equipment will cause our weapons systems to perform below expectations. The impacts would range from premature mechanical failures due to incorrectly installed mechanical components, to radar and missile operational inaccuracies due to improperly set components. A defined, multi-year modernization plan for test equipment is in place. The Calibration Standards (M6005) funding is provided to execute a detailed, multi-year sustainment and modernization plan for Calibration Standards employed at intermediate, organizational, and depot level maintenance activities. Calibration Standards are equipment employed to ensure the accuracy of test equipment used to install, align, and maintain all Navy weapons systems ashore and afloat. The Navy's inventory of Calibration Standards is approaching obsolescence and require modernization to avoid deterioration in the accuracy and calibration of our weapons systems. Many of the original standards are no longer in production, so replacement standards must be purchased from newer model inventory, some of which have a greater unit cost. A defined, multi-year modernization plan for Calibration Standards is in place. Several multi-year contracts requirements have been initiated and several more packages are in process. Procuring the planned calibration standards supports the performance of every Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA) weapon system including Nuclear Reactor Program maintenance, the Aegis Weapon System afloat and Aegis Ashore Romania/Poland, AN/APX-72 IFF transponder, AN/BRD-7 ECM Intercept System, AN/SQQ-34 ASW Module, and all afloat radio systems. The 2960 Line Item (LI) is shared between the Strike Force Interoperability (SFI) and Shipboard Electronic Systems Evaluation Facilities (SESEF) programs. This program supports various Navy Land Based Test Sites (LBTS) required to support integration and interoperability testing. Sites include, but are not limited to, Naval Surface Warfare Center (NSWC) Dahlgren, Surface Combat System Center (SCSC) Wallops Island, Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific, and NSWC Dam Neck. This funding also supports the Shipboard Electronic Systems Evaluation Facilities (SESEF) Program for the procurement, installation for upgrades and modernization to provide electromagnetic system test and evaluation services to afloat and shore commands for development of new and upgraded systems, to validate system performance following new construction and overhaul, and to provide real-time assessment of material readiness in an operational environment. The United States Navy has a requirement to fully test and certify computer programs for maturity, Interoperability and Integration (I&I) prior to delivery to the Fleet. Commander, U.S. Fleet Forces Command (CUSFFC) provided specific direction to develop a unified modernization process and certify all combat system baselines for integration and interoperability as an integral step in the Chief of Naval Operations (CNO) Optimized Fleet Response Plan (OFRP).
